html:
Chimor was the kingdom of the Chimú people on the north coast of Peru, ruled from the great adobe city of Chan Chan from about 900 until the Inca conquered it around 1470. At its height it ran some 1,000 km along the coast, the largest state of its time in the Andes.

The Chimú rose in the Moche valley, the old heartland of the Moche. Their own tradition said a founder named Taycanamo came from the sea on a balsa raft, and that his son and grandson conquered the valleys around. Later kings added the Sicán lands to the north.

Chan Chan was the largest adobe city in the Americas. Its centre held about ten huge walled compounds, often seen as palaces of successive kings, each with storerooms, courts and a burial platform. The walls carry relief friezes of fish, birds and waves. Chimú wealth rested on long canals that carried water between valleys, and on skilled metalworkers who made objects of gold and silver.

Chimor was the last state with any chance of stopping the Inca. Topa Inca Yupanqui defeated its king Minchançaman in the 1470s and took him to Cusco, along with many Chimú goldsmiths. Their skill and their ideas of royal rule shaped the empire that swallowed them.
